entities.summary:
Charles III of Alençon was a French nobleman of the Capetian House of Valois, born on 01 February 1337 and died on 13 July 1375. He was count of Alençon and Perche from 1346 until 1361, when he became a Dominican friar, and archbishop of Lyon from 1365 until his death. His tenure as count was marked by power struggles with neighboring lords, while his time as archbishop saw significant efforts to reform the church.


 As a prominent figure in medieval French politics, Charles III's relationships with other nobles and clergy are well-documented. He collaborated with King Louis XI of France, while also participating in the Lyon Cathedral construction project. Additionally, Charles III's influence extended to the surrounding region, with his rule over Alençon and Perche contributing to the cultural and economic development of the area.


 Despite his significant impact, Charles III's legacy is often overshadowed by that of his contemporaries. Nevertheless, his contributions to the church and the region remain an important part of medieval French history.


 The cultural footprint of Charles III can be seen in the numerous architectural and artistic projects he commissioned during his tenure as archbishop, including the renovation of the Lyon Cathedral.


 The irony of Charles III's fate lies in the contrast between his life of luxury and his eventual decision to become a Dominican friar, reflecting the complexities of medieval spirituality and the search for meaning in a world of conflicting values.
